originShared.text: Florida's Reciprocity form (DBPR CILB 32) covers applicants from Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina in General, Building, and Residential categories; it has no Air-Conditioning category, so reciprocity is not available to HVAC contractors in Florida.
The route is DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes), which lists Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning among its license categories.

Within CILB 10, the NASCLA-based Option A does not apply to this classification: the form restricts it to "General, Building, and Residential license" only. The route is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years, of a license type "the same or similar as the license type being applied for".

Options A (substantially equivalent exam) and B (substantially equivalent licensing criteria) also exist, but CILB 10 warns that comparisons of state-specific tests are "very stringent and rarely approved".
For Option C, submit verification of licensure from your state showing at least 10 years and any disciplinary action, and a copy of your state's statutes or rules defining your license type.

Open question: CILB 10's 2-hour Florida Building Code course is required of General, Building, Residential, and Roofing Contractor applicants; Air-Conditioning is not listed, and the document does not say whether Air-Conditioning applicants face it.
